item.title: EasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US firm
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjejzjpy98wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
EasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US firm - Published No-frills airline EasyJet has agreed to be taken over in a £5.7bn deal by US firm Apollo after a rival bidder dropped out. The takeover was agreed after US investment firm Castlelake, which had made a series of offers for the carrier, said it was withdrawing from the bid battle. Apollo said it wants to help the airline grow and that it does not intend to cut any jobs in the first 12 months after the takeover has been completed, implying that passengers can expect largely the same service. EasyJet is one of Europe's largest airlines. It employs more than 19,000 people, and flies around 1,200 routes across 35 European countries. It was founded by Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou in 1995 to offer cheap air fares to Europe from the UK. Its first flights took off in November 1995 flying from Luton to Glasgow and Edinburgh, with its first international flights the following year. Sir Stelios and his family still own around 15% of the business, and he said he supported Apollo's plans for the airline "to create more growth". "My family and I intend to remain invested as long-term major shareholders of EasyJet for the next chapter in the company's journey," he said in a statement. The future ownership of EasyJet has been uncertain since it emerged in late May that Castlelake was considering a bid for the airline. Castlelake made a number of approaches for EasyJet, which were rebuffed initially after the carrier accused the US firm of trying to buy it "on the cheap". In early July, EasyJet and Castlelake said they had agreed a deal in principle, but then Apollo - which owns Wagamama parent The Restaurant Group - swooped in with a higher bid. Under the offer from Apollo, EasyJet shareholders will receive £7.15 per share. AJ Bell's head of financial analysis, Danni Hewson said while the offer was significantly above where the company's shares were trading before the Iran war, the figure was "still woefully short of the company's pre-pandemic highs". Apollo said it was "highly supportive" of the airline's existing strategy, adding there was "a significant opportunity to accelerate the operational and commercial ambitions" for the EasyJet Group. "EasyJet is a leader in European aviation, having built a differentiated market position through its compelling customer proposition, expansive network and strong brand," said Alex van Hoek, partner and European private equity lead at Apollo. EasyJet chief executive Kenton Jarvis said "We welcome Apollo's commitment to our business and our people, and believe that its experience in the aviation sector makes it a strong partner for EasyJet." The deal will still need to win approval from regulators, including in the EU where rules mean EasyJet's owners will have to be majority EU-based. Apollo anticipates this can be achieved by making the Haji-Ioannou family, and other EU-based shareholders, owners of around half of the business. Apollo said though it does not intend to cut any staff for at least 12 months after the deal goes through, if the deal completes and EasyJet delists from the stock exchange to become a private company, some jobs related to maintaining its public-listed operations could go. The firm said that would be a "limited number of roles in specific areas." AJ Bell's Hewson said the potential loss of another well-known name from London markets will be seen as a blow. "Air travel might not be as sexy as space travel, but retail investors understand it and names like EasyJet can't easily be replaced," she said.

item.title: Iran says deal with Oman on Strait of Hormuz is in final stages
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg9d3eyeggo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Iran says deal with Oman on Strait of Hormuz is in final stages - Published Iran says it has reached an agreement with Oman on a route for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei did not give any further details on the agreement, which he said was "in the final stages". Baqaei warned, however, that a deal with Oman would not guarantee safe navigation through the strait, arguing security remained impacted by the US blockade of Iran's ports. The US and Oman have not commented on the proposal. Since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, Tehran has largely blocked the Strait of Hormuz through which about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas usually passes. On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump warned that Iran would be "hit very hard" if the strait did not open "very soon". His comments came after senior US officials said talks had progressed to allow shipments to potentially resume later this week, though Iran has maintained that it is not negotiating with the US and has no plans to do so. Reopening the strait has been a key point in discussions between the two countries and mediators. In his statement, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman said the "geographical coordinates of the route" had been agreed with Oman. "The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," he said, according to Iran's official Irna news agency. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi later told Irna the new route would be temporary and could stay open from two to four months. He did not give further details. Oil prices edged lower on Thursday, with global benchmark Brent crude down by 0.3% at $79.24 (£58.84) in morning Asian trade. Energy prices have fluctuated wildly during the conflict as shipments through the key route for around 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) have been severely disrupted. Since the beginning of the war, traffic through the strait has dwindled. Iran has said all passage needs to be cleared beforehand - and it has attacked vessels which have ignored the order. One of the main points of disagreement between Tehran and Washington has been Iran's threat to impose a fee on vessels wishing to cross the strait. Iran is seeking fees of between 5% and 7% of the price of cargoes from ships using the strait, according to a senior Iranian official cited by Reuters. Oman is discussing fees of around 3%, while Washington wants no fees at all. The proposed deal would also give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. In June, Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), aiming to stop fighting, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and reach agreement to end the war within 60 days. The deal quickly fell through, as did diplomatic talks, with tit-for-tat attacks resuming just days after the MoU was signed. The US has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports in the region, while another blockade is in place on Saudi Arabia's ports in the Red Sea, imposed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since 20 July. The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel and US-allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's then Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in that first attack, after which he was succeeded by his son Mojtaba Khamenei. The younger Khamenei was wounded in the same strikes that launched the war and has not appeared in public since. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Wednesday that communication with Khamenei was "difficult at the moment". "In any case, his presence is a very great source of strength for us so that we can continue," Pezeshkian said, according to state media. The younger Khamenei, who did not appear at his father's funeral ceremonies last month, has communicated through written statements but his low profile has led to speculation about his relations with other top officials. Pezeshkian insisted he had been able to hold productive meetings with him and been met with "kindness and very sound logic". "Unfortunately, the current situation allows some malicious people to describe him differently and to present a different image of him," he said.

item.title: Indian journalist Tarun Tejpal sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2v551w9v8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Indian journalist Tarun Tejpal sentenced to 10 years in jail for rape - Published An Indian court has sentenced former Tehelka magazine editor Tarun Tejpal to 10 years in prison for raping a former colleague, overturning his 2021 acquittal in a decade-old case. The Goa bench of the Bombay High Court convicted Tejpal under sections of Indian law pertaining to rape and sexual harassment. Along with jail terms which run concurrently, the court has also ordered him to pay fines adding up to more than 1mn rupees ($10,500; £7,800). Tejpal, who has denied the accusations, said before the sentencing that he would file an appeal in the Supreme Court. The allegations against Tejpal, one of India's best-known editors, had made national headlines in 2013. A year before that, thousands of Indians had participated in protests after a brutal gang rape and murder of a woman in Delhi, leading to a larger conversation on sexual violence. Tejpal's accuser, who cannot be identified under Indian law, said that he sexually assaulted her in a lift during Tehelka's high-profile international conference in Goa in November 2013, an event attended by, among others, Hollywood star Robert De Niro. Tejpal initially blamed the assault on "a lapse of judgement" and "a misreading of the situation" which had "led to an unfortunate incident that rails against all we believe in and fight for". But as the case escalated, he issued a statement urging authorities to examine the CCTV footage "so the accurate version of events stands clearly revealed". He also alleged that the case against him was part of a "political vendetta" by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government in Goa. Tehelka, the magazine Tejpal co-founded in 2000, had published a number of scoops, many of them based on sting operations. Some of these stories - including Operation West End in which some of its journalists posed as arms dealers, secretly filming senior army officials, bureaucrats and even the president of the then ruling BJP taking bribes to push through a fake deal - created national and international ripples. Tejpal was arrested in 2013 and spent seven months in jail until the Supreme Court granted him bail. In 2021, a sessions court in Goa threw out all the charges against him. But the judge's observations in the 527-page order sparked criticism after she questioned the behaviour of the survivor.. In photographs taken shortly after the assault, the judge wrote, the young woman was "smiling and looked happy, normal, in [a] good mood". "She did not look disturbed, reserved, terrified or traumatised in any way even though this was immediately after she claims to have been sexually assaulted," the order said. The Goa government had appealed against the acquittal in the high court. Appearing for the Goa government, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta had urged the high court to impose the maximum sentence on Tejpal. "This court must give a clear message to society that when a girl says no, it means no," Livelaw quoted him as saying. "All I can say is I am 62. I believe I am a political victim. I am a father of two daughters. I have a wife. All we can say is we will go up and appeal. My lawyer wants me to request you to be lenient," legal website Bar and Bench quoted Tejpal as telling the court before the sentencing. Tejpal was found guilty under legal sections including 376(2)(f), which pertains to rape committed by "a relative, guardian or teacher of, or a person in a position of trust or authority towards the woman".

Rihanna is 'in the studio', says partner A$AP Rocky - Published Rihanna could be set to break a decade-long album hiatus, according to her partner A$AP Rocky. "She in the studio right now," the rapper said on the The Jason Lee podcast on Wednesday. Few details about the project were revealed, apart from a denial that the pair would collaborate on a double album. However, in response to questioning about about a potential new album, he added "she cooking." The singer and beauty mogul from Barbados, whose real name is Robyn Fenty, has not released a full album since 2016's Anti. "Are you the reason we don't have an album?" podcaster Jason Lee asked the rapper on his show, noting the three children shared by the pair and Rihanna's travel. The rapper denied this, instead saying that the singer was in fact working on new music. "Yeah I said it, sorry babe," he continued, adding that he would "get in trouble for this." Little other information about the possible music was revealed in the interview. In February last year, Rihanna said that she felt "really optimistic" about a new album. "I feel like I've finally cracked it, girl!," she told a reporter from Harper's Bazaar. She also said, "I cannot put up anything mediocre. After waiting eight years, you might as well just wait some more." Since her last album, Rihanna has released singles, including some linked to film projects, including 2022's Lift Me Up for Black Panther: Wakanda Forever. She has also launched multiple businesses, including her popular makeup range Fenty Beauty and a lingerie company. The 38-year-old's net worth has been estimated by Forbes at over a billion dollars. During the interview, A$AP Rocky, real name Rakim Mayers, refused to comment on whether he and Rihanna had married. item.title: Outrage as Ugandan football captain beaten to death in street gang attack
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2g0038yr8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Outrage as Ugandan football captain beaten to death in street gang attack - Published Ugandans are mourning the death at 27 of one of the country's best-known footballers after he was beaten by suspected robbers near his home in the capital, Kampala. Police said David Owori was fatally assaulted after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings, prompting an outpouring of grief and renewed public anger over violent crime in Uganda. Owori captained Sports Club (SC) Villa, the Uganda Premier League record champions, where he played both as a right-back and midfielder. He also represented the country's national team - the Cranes. "We have lost more than a player - we have lost a leader, brother and friend," SC Villa said in a statement. Witnesses said a group of attackers hit the footballer with paving stones on Tuesday night before robbing Owori of his belongings and fleeing, leaving him unconscious. SC Villa spokesperson Asan Kasingye told journalists that Owori was targeted just outside his home in Makindye, a Kampala suburb. "The player was ambushed by thugs as he approached his home, leaving him with life-threatening injuries before he was rushed to the medical facility," Kasingye said. Owori was rushed to a nearby medical clinic and then transferred to a private facility in the city, but he died of his injuries on Wednesday. Local police spokesperson Rachael Kawala said detectives were pursuing leads to identify those responsible. "The scene of the incident has been documented and processed to ensure that all relevant evidence is collected and preserved," Kawala added. Owori's murder has sent shockwaves across Uganda, with the football community, including fans and teammates, and politicians demanding justice. Tributes are continuing to pour in for the defender, who was popularly known as Colgate. The Federation of Uganda Football Associations (Fufa) described Owori as "a true leader on and off the pitch". "David was not just a footballer. He was both a leader and an inspiration to a generation," it said in a statement. The national side, the Cranes, said the team had lost a football star who "carried the hopes" of Uganda. Parliament on Wednesday observed a minute's silence in honour of Owori and called for a quick investigation. The versatile player, renowned for his tactical discipline and ability to feature across midfield, returned to SC Villa in 2023 - after two years in Europe - for a second spell. At the time of his death, he was among the longest-serving members of the current squad. He helped lead the high-profile team to their first league title in 20 years securing a record 17th top-flight crown in 2024. His influence on and off the pitch earned him a contract extension until January 2027 with the team. Owori also featured in the national team during the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign and was regarded as a strong contender for future call-ups to the Cranes. His death has triggered anger on social media, with many Ugandans questioning the level of violent crime in Kampala and calling for tougher action against criminals. item.title: Boxer charged with killing aid worker in Athens after his wife gave police 'key' details
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj6390k0e26o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Boxer charged with killing aid worker in Athens after his wife gave police 'key' details - Published An Afghan boxer was accused of killing a Scottish aid worker in Greece after his wife gave "key" details to police, the BBC has been told. Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, has been charged with homicide with intent – equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law - alongside robbery and weapons offences. The body of Elisabeth Ross, who was 38, was discovered in a suitcase by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of Athens on 18 July. Ahmadzai's wife, Alaina Hall, is said to have given information to police, including location data which placed her husband and Ross at the same apartment on 15 July – the day Ross is thought to have been killed. - Family's tribute to 'kind and selfless' aid worker killed in Greece - Published15 hours ago Appearing in court earlier, Ahmadzai asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges. His lawyer, Christos Erdas, said his client had exercised his right to remain silent, and that his rights had been "violated" through leaks of evidence and documents from the case file - including his right to the presumption of innocence. The lawyer said that when Ross was found, she had no injuries and any apparent cause of death was "entirely absent". He said his client wanted the forensic medical report and the "toxicological and histological examinations of the deceased" to be included in the case file. Erdas added: "His [Ahmadzai's] stance towards the prosecuting and investigating authorities did not constitute a stance of denial but, on the contrary, one of reservation, so that he may present his defence in full once the case file has been completed with the above essential documents – which were not sought by the preliminary investigating authorities – with the sole aim of establishing the substantive truth for both sides." Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months. Ahmadzai was initially detained on illegal weapons possession charges and is facing a charge of homicide with intent, as well as allegations that he stole more than €10,000 (£8,500) from the victim's bank accounts using her bank cards. The police union in Greece said that initially, the coroner's report cited an undetermined cause of death, as the body showed no signs of external trauma. It said following a more detailed investigation, autopsy and post-mortem examination, "asphyxiation was listed as the probable cause of death". The union has now told the BBC that officers arrested the accused after his wife provided them with "key" and "decisive" details. Officers involved with the case said these details included sharing a location-tracking app, which placed both Ahmadzai and Ross at the same apartment. Hall, who has a child with Ahmadzai, told police that she and her husband met Elisabeth – known as Lisa - while volunteering for a refugee charity in Athens in February 2026. She described the victim as a "very pleasant and sweet person, kind-hearted, with a good soul". Hall claimed that after the three had gone on a walk, her husband remained in touch with Ross for several days. The aid worker is believed to have asked Ahmadzai to help deliver bibles. Court documents claim that on 15 July, Hall said she saw a text message sent from Ross to Ahmadzai which read: "Thank you for your intention to come with me." Hall claimed in a statement that she awoke later that night to find that her husband had left their home without warning. She is quoted as saying: "I checked his location on my cell phone. I saw that he was inside the apartment on Rethymno Street. "I was surprised because there was no particular reason for him to be there at that time." She claimed her husband told her that he was watching football at a café and headed to the apartment to use the toilet – which she initially believed but no longer did. Hall said that in the days that followed, her husband appeared to be particularly upset, blaming the death of a relative in India. She said he suggested they leave the city unexpectedly. She said after this, her husband appeared to be happy once again, bought her a new iPhone 17 Pro and later gave her €2,550 (£2,180). Hall said he could not "convincingly" explain where this money came from. When news broke that a woman had been found dead inside a suitcase close to where the couple lived, Hall said she woke up in the middle of the night on 29 July and thought it could be Ross. She told investigators that after messaging the aid worker, the replies "were not in Lisa's style both in terms of her level of English and the use of emojis that she never used". She said this prompted her to become concerned that Ross could be the woman in the suitcase. She told police: "All of the above made me feel strange. Especially combining the dates, the messages and my husband's behaviour. "I have various thoughts that make me feel uncomfortable." After the body was identified, Hall said she received threatening messages with photos of herself and her baby. She told police she became so afraid that she and Ahmadzai left their home and spent the night in different places. The BBC has been told Ahmadzai denies homicide with intent but admits moving the body, claiming that he did so because he feared he would be blamed for her death. A statement from the police's organised crime directorate said Ahmadzai was brought to a police station on 30 July. "In particular, it emerged that the 26-year-old placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned site," the statement said. Ahmadzai is accused of killing Ross, then sending a series of messages from her phone to her friends and family before switching off the device. Greek newspapers Proto Thema and Ta Nea have reported that he bought a phone and texted Ross's friends in Athens, impersonating an unnamed jihadist saying he had killed the Scot because of her religion. The newspapers reported his wife told the police she suspected her husband's involvement in the killing when she woke up to find he was not in their apartment and tracked his phone to where Ross was staying. Police said Ross - who is from Edinburgh and is known to family and friends as Lisa - had been volunteering with a refugee support group based in Athens. She arrived in Greece on 26 June and stayed in the Keratsini area of Piraeus until 10 July. Ross is believed to have died a number of days before she was found. Greek officials contacted Interpol and American authorities were able to identify her fingerprints. The investigation was carried out by Greece's organised crime directorate. item.title: Air India's new CEO faces financial and safety turbulence
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9987kkrnl5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Air India's new CEO faces financial and safety turbulence - Published Air India has appointed a new chief executive as the airline grapples with mounting challenges, including heavy financial losses and the fallout from last year's crash that killed 260 people. Tewolde Gebremariam succeeds Campbell Wilson, who stepped down from the role in April. Gebremariam was earlier CEO at Ethiopian Airlines, where he worked for over a decade, growing the regional carrier into one of Africa's largest airlines. Air India, which Tata Group bought from the Indian government in 2022, has been dealing with a period of operational turbulence. The airline operates a fleet of 198 aircraft, flying nearly 5,000 weekly flights to 91 destinations in India and abroad, according to the Air India website. Air India said Gebremariam was unanimously chosen by its board after an extensive search, citing his leadership and operational expertise to steer the airline's "next phase of growth". N Chandrasekaran, Air India chairman, said: "Having completed the initial phase of stabilisation, integration, and fleet commitments under Campbell's guidance, Air India is now entering a critical execution and expansion era." Wilson, a former Singapore Airlines executive hired after Tata Group bought Air India nearly four years ago, had signalled in 2024 that he planned to step down in 2026 and had been preparing the airline for a smooth transition. Now, his replacement Gebremariam has said that he is looking forward to building a "world-class global airline" that "reflects India's extraordinary economic potential". During his tenure at Ethiopian Airlines, Gebremariam was credited with expanding the fleet nearly threefold and growing it into Africa's most profitable airline. At Air India, however, Gebremariam faces a daunting task. He takes over as the airline grapples with a series of safety and operational challenges, led by last June's fatal Ahmedabad-London crash, a major setback to its ambitions. The final crash report is due in October. The airline has continued to struggle since returning to private ownership, reporting a record loss of nearly $2.3bn (£1.7bn) last month. Chandrasekaran has warned a turnaround could take up to a decade. The airline has also cut nearly a third of its international operations. The airline has also made headlines for a string of operational setbacks. In March, a Delhi-Vancouver flight turned back after nearly eight hours because it lacked clearance to enter Canadian airspace. These troubles come as India's wider aviation sector faces pressure from rising costs, disrupted international routes due to the Iran war, aircraft delivery delays and tighter regulatory scrutiny. Aviation experts told the BBC that Gebremariam may be the leader Air India needs, pointing to two defining crises he steered Ethiopian Airlines through: the 2019 Boeing 737 Max crash that killed 157 people and the Covid pandemic, when the airline stayed profitable by expanding its cargo business as passenger revenues collapsed. "Gebremariam endeared himself to his employees during both these black swan events, especially his backing of the pilots and engineers at Ethiopian," Sanjay Lazar, CEO of Avialaz Consultants, told the BBC. At Air India, Gebremariam's priorities will include rebuilding workplace culture, lifting employee morale, accelerating delayed fleet expansion and refurbishment, and reshaping the airline's network to stem losses, experts say. Air India has not said when he will take over, saying details will be announced later.

item.title: Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr7kldz4djno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity - Published Warning: This story contains details some may find distressing A 17-year-old Sudanese girl holds a young child in her arms with a heavy calm that belies her age and the concerns she has for his future. "This son of mine has no father, no birth certificate and no national number," Amira, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, tells the BBC. Looking down at him, she speaks slowly as if still trying to grasp the details of what has happened to her since the civil war erupted in Sudan. She and her family used to live in the eastern neighbourhoods of el-Fasher, a city that came under siege from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in a brutal power struggle with the military since April 2023. El-Fasher was the army's last stronghold in the western region of Darfur until it fell to the RSF and allied Arab militias after 18 months last October. For the tens of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city, it was a nightmare – with constant bombardment, clashes and suffering from a lack of food. In the end Amira and her family decided to flee early in 2025, desperate to find a safer area. But as they snuck out on a road south-west of the city, she says she was abducted by three armed men from the RSF and held captive. "They blindfolded me and took me to the Tabit area south of el-Fasher. I was locked in a room for two months, and every day one of them raped me in turn," she recounts in a low voice After weeks in captivity, she discovered she was pregnant and became very sick. Amira says when the men wanted to get rid of her, they dropped her near the area she had been captured. It was with the help of other people fleeing el-Fasher that she was taken to receive medical help. Months later, at a humanitarian hub that was not under RSF control, she gave birth at a hospital run by the International Medical Corps. There she received some support from a Sudanese aid organisation - the Nada Al-Azhar Foundation for Disaster Prevention and Sustainable Development (Nada). The group was also able to find her family, who had made it to a camp where hundreds of thousands of people from el-Fasher have sought refuge. It was a huge relief for them all to be reunited, but the family still face challenges - one being that eight months after giving birth, Amira has been unable to register her son's birth. "Even getting a birth notification from the hospital requires information that doesn't exist," says Amira, explaining that she is unable to provide any details about the child's father. Without this she cannot organise any official recognition of the baby's legal identity. "I can't get him vaccinated, or enrol him in nursery or school," she says. "I'm afraid for his future because he isn't registered at all. My economic situation is very difficult, and I can't afford his treatment or care. I can't even go to work for fear of being exposed to violence again." According to Nada, Amira's story is not an isolated case, but part of a reality repeated in areas experiencing conflict across Sudan. This is because many children are being born in complex circumstances, often without the knowledge of the father - meaning their births cannot be registered, explains Abu Bakr Yousif Yaqoub, Nada's director of protection programmes. "Registering a child requires identity information, a national number and a birth certificate. But when the father is absent or unknown, it becomes extremely difficult," he tells the BBC from el-Fasher. "The mother is often alone, and sometimes she herself is still a child who needs care, which limits her ability to care for her baby. "There are also health challenges related to the lack of follow-up on essential vaccinations, which begin at birth and continue through the child's early years." He warns that this situation does not just affect a child's early years but extends to their future education and as an adult being able to travel or obtain official documents. It is not easy to obtain data about the number of children that have been born as a result of rape in Sudan. According to Nada's director general, Shaza Ahmed, this comes down to social stigma as the true numbers are not recorded. "Women who experience such assaults do not feel comfortable reporting them," she tells the BBC, speaking from Port Sudan, an army-held city in the east of Sudan. "Unfortunately, most of the mothers of these children are themselves children - girls under the age of 18. Therefore, they cannot make the decision to go officially to court or the police, as they need a guardian to accompany them." She notes that 90% of the cases recorded by her organisation involve families refusing to allow official reporting of the sexual assaults that led to pregnancy. "As a Sudanese woman, my greatest fear and concern for children born as a result of rape is that we are facing a whole generation that will live under stigma, danger and fear," Ahmed says. "These children will not receive respect from society, their well-being will not be truly protected, and above all, they will not have access to services or their rights." For Ahmed they are not being treated as if they are "fully human", even though Sudanese law does grant all children the right to obtain an identity. Sudanese lawyer Majida Idris explains that the Child Act of 2010 allows for the registration of children born outside marriage. But it relies on the mother being willing to file a report that she has been assaulted - because this kick starts the registration process. Once reported, the case is then referred to social services for documentation, before being sent to the civil registry, where the child is registered under the mother's name and given a full legal name according to procedures. However, Idris says that the reality during war is completely different, especially in Darfur, where the ongoing conflict has led to the collapse of civil services and the shutdown of civil registry offices, leaving thousands of children unregistered. "The absence of documents does not just mean the absence of a piece of paper - it means denying the child access to education, healthcare and legal recognition," she tells the BBC. The lawyer says it is imperative to reactivate civil registry offices in accessible areas and intensify legal efforts to ensure children obtain their right to identity and legal recognition. Amira and her child remain in Darfur - and therefore in administrative limbo. Her mother admits that the lack of paperwork for her grandson is a worry. Yet for the moment the family is overwhelmed with gratitude to have found one another again. Amira has also been offered emotional and psychological support sessions and other advice by Nada - which is a comfort to the family. "I was so extremely worried until I found her. I hadn't been eating or drinking," Amira's mother told the BBC. "The reunion was like a miracle from God. To see our daughter back sitting among us is a gift and blessing that could not be thanked enough for." item.title: 'Put your phone down': K-pop band weighs in on concert etiquette
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39ep3p0ld1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Put your phone down': K-pop band weighs in on concert etiquette - Published Kicking off their global tour in the South Korean city of Incheon, the five members of K-pop boy band Cortis saunter onto stage in casual, streetwear-inspired outfits, exuding an effortlessly cool vibe. "Put your phone down," one of the members bellows. Piercing screams erupt. A sea of illuminated screens flickers back. "I told you, put your phone down," he repeats, louder this time. Some fans do just that, but the packed stadium vibrates harder with cheers as thousands of phones stay in the air. It's hard to say how serious this theatrical command is. "Put your phone down" is also the name of Cortis's ongoing concert tour, which started in Incheon on 18 July and will head to cities like New York and Los Angeles before returning to Seoul later this month. The refrain reflects a message the band has long pushed: that fans should stop watching concerts through six-inch screens and engage with their performances in real life. It's drawn mixed reactions from their fandom: fan-filmed content is a valuable social currency in K-pop. Park Ji-yeon, for one, could not bring herself to stop recording Cortis's performances. The 22-year-old had specially rented a new, top-tier smartphone for both days of the Cortis concert just so she could film in the highest quality. "I was standing right at the front, and I couldn't bring myself to put my phone down because I don't know if I'll ever get this opportunity again," she tells the BBC. "I usually film concerts because I know a lot of those memories will fade as soon as I leave the venue." While fans like Park continued to film, some heeded the band's call. Kim Ga-eun, 25, who was seated in the amphitheatre-style venue, saw it all. "People in the back of the standing section were having a great time dancing together. I thought that really reflected the intention behind the concert," she says. Cortis has had a whirlwind year since debuting last year under record label BigHit Music - part of the company that created pop sensation BTS. Most of its members are teenagers. The oldest of the group, James, is just 20 years old. Their music videos have each amassed millions of views. Over the weekend they performed at Lollapalooza, the famed music festival in Chicago. The band's name, Cortis, is derived from the phrase "colour outside the lines", which according to their record label is meant to encapsulate the band's free spirit and refusal to conform to societal rules - which, in this case, appears to include telling fans to resist the temptation of the phone camera. They join a prominent wave of artists around the world who have been advocating the same. Singers like Phoebe Bridgers and Alicia Keys have required their concert attendees to use lock pouches - sealed bags that allow people to hold on to their phones without being able to access them. Few have gone as far as British rock group Suede, whose frontman Brett Anderson leapt over a barricade during a 2023 performance in Singapore to grab at fans' phones. Billie Eilish, who has defended filming as a way for fans to relive precious memories after a show, gently cooed to her front row audience during a performance in Amsterdam: "Put your phone down, I'm right here." Even BTS, K-pop's golden boys, have made similar requests. "Stop looking at your phone screen. Just look at me," BTS member Jungkook teased the audience at one concert. "From the artists' perspective, interacting with fans is a really important part of performing, so I think they want people to focus more on that than on their phones," Park says of Cortis's anti-mobile rallying cry. After all, fancams - zoomed-in videos focusing on a single celebrity - are a prized currency in K-pop communities. Once shared online, people meticulously study the choreography in them and delight in catching subtle movements and expressions by their favourite band members. These clips live on as fodder for collective swooning and fan-made montages. And this is why Cortis's incessant calls to for people to put their phones down have rubbed some the wrong way - in a fan culture that's obsessed with capturing every moment. After the first day of their concert, disgruntled comments emerged online among fans. "I spent over one million won ($700; £520) attending both days," Park says, referring to the sum of not just concert tickets but also additional expenses like transport and accommodation. "I think a lot of fans spent similar amounts of money, so constantly hearing them asking us to put our phones down made some fans even more frustrated." These murmurs appear to have reached Cortis, who fans say dialled down their message on the second day of the concert. "On the first day, the message felt more like, 'Let's put our phones down and have fun together.' On the second day, it changed slightly to, 'We understand why you want to film, so let's just make sure we enjoy ourselves together,'" Kim recalls. "They said filming was okay, but they wanted us to enjoy the concert together, and that 'Put Your Phone Down' was more of a mindset."

item.title: India is a nation of walkers - but its cities forgot them
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce3e4enkrqro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
India is a nation of walkers - but its cities forgot them - Published For much of my life, walking in Indian cities has felt less like exercising a right than negotiating an obstacle course. I grew up in Kolkata, where wide pavements disappeared beneath rows of hawkers. I moved to Delhi, where roads seemed designed almost exclusively for cars. Now I live in Gurugram, where footpaths vanish into rubble and garbage, are abruptly blocked by parked vehicles or construction, or sit uncomfortably high above the road. So when India's Supreme Court declared in June that the right to walk safely on designated footpaths was a fundamental right, external, it felt less like judicial activism than common sense arriving decades late. Walking is the most democratic form of transport. Yet it is also the one India's cities have neglected most consistently. It's remarkable because India remains, above all, a nation of walkers. Around 45 million people walk to work every day, according to census-based estimates, compared with only about 5.4 million who commute in private cars, jeeps or vans. Nearly a third of urban workers walk to work, while virtually every bus or metro journey begins and ends on foot. Add school runs, shopping trips and other everyday journeys, and walking dominates urban mobility. A 2019 survey of selected cities found that 63% of all journeys were made on foot, making pedestrians the single largest group of road users. Many are what researchers call "captive pedestrians" - people who walk not by choice but because they cannot afford another option. Women are especially dependent on walking. Yet the people who contribute least to congestion and pollution often face the greatest risks. The evidence is harrowing. Even where pavements exist, they are often broken, narrow or inaccessible to older people, children and those with disabilities. They are also blocked by motorcycles, swallowed by parked cars, encroachments or excavated for utility works. Faded zebra crossings are treated as little more than road markings no-one respects. Flyovers speed traffic while forcing pedestrians into hazardous detours below. A landmark 2011 study of six Indian cities found that India's streets routinely fail pedestrians because of "poor and unsafe" infrastructure. The Walkability in Indian Cities report by the Clean Air Initiative for Asian Cities (CAI-Asia) gave the surveyed cities a median walkability score of just 47 out of 100, with the worst conditions around public transport terminals - ironically the places where most journeys begin and end on foot As Geetam Tiwari, a transport scholar at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi puts it, pedestrians have been "pushed to the margins of the road networks" forcing them to "jostle for space with motor vehicles". The price is paid in lives. Officially pedestrians account for roughly a fifth of road deaths, external, but independent studies cited by Tiwari estimate the share is closer to 30-40%. Pedestrians are also the second-largest group of road accident victims after two-wheeler riders. In Delhi and Mumbai, they account for more than half of all road deaths. According to a World Bank study, crashes already cost India an estimated 3-5% of its GDP each year through lost productivity, healthcare costs and disability. The Supreme Court case arose from one such tragedy: a five-year-old boy crushed by a truck while walking to school with his father. The judges responded with unusual eloquence. Walking, Justice PS Narasimha wrote, is "the simplest of the simple human activity, inextricably connected to life". Roads therefore impose a corresponding duty on the state to provide safe footpaths. "The fundamental right to walk on demarcated footpaths shall override the privilege of a motorised vehicle," he declared. The judgment challenges decades of Indian urban planning, where progress has often been measured in kilometres of expressways, flyovers and elevated corridors. Streets were engineered to move vehicles as quickly as possible, while the one road user every citizen inevitably becomes - the pedestrian - largely disappeared from planners' imagination. "People know about the latest cars, but walking has become invisible," says Rishi Aggarwal, who has spent more than a decade trying to change that mindset in Mumbai. Through city walks and public talks, his advocacy group, Walking Project, encourages residents to notice what they have stopped seeing: broken pavements, blocked crossings and unsafe junctions - and compare them with the standards pedestrians are entitled to expect. "When people become apathetic, they stop observing the street," he says. In a city where an estimated 15 million walking trips are made every day, Aggarwal argues, it is not just footpaths that have disappeared from view, but also the millions of people who depend on them. For Rahul Goel, a transportation researcher at Delhi's Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), the problem begins with governance. "Are footpaths maintained and cleaned? Does the city ensure they aren't encroached upon?" he says. "In Delhi, many roads do have footpaths, but they're often unusable because of poor governance." Poor design makes matters worse. Cars parked perpendicular to the kerb often conceal footpaths or block them altogether, while vehicles parked directly on pavements are a common sight. Footpaths are often too narrow for the number of pedestrians. Many are so high above the road that older people, wheelchair users and others with limited mobility struggle to use them. Others end abruptly, forcing people back onto the carriageway. "If the footpath is discontinuous, it's simply more convenient to keep walking on the road," says Goel. He believes the deeper problem is one of priorities. "Urban transport governance is still centred on moving vehicles. Reducing congestion and maximising road space for motor traffic take precedence over pedestrians," he says. Civic agencies are often reluctant to widen footpaths because they view carriageway space as sacrosanct. That mindset, Goel argues, is reinforced by public pressure. Traffic jams dominate headlines and social media, pushing authorities to keep vehicles moving. In Delhi, many mid-block crossings have been replaced by U-turns to reduce stoppages, forcing pedestrians onto foot overbridges. "People don't just need to walk along a road," says Goel. "They need to be able to cross it safely too." The result is a stark urban inequality. In Gurugram, a high-speed arterial road cuts through busy neighbourhoods with few safe crossings. Domestic workers, labourers and other pedestrians routinely dodge speeding traffic, and many are killed trying to cross. Only after the death toll mounted did authorities begin building footbridges. Across India's cities, those who cannot afford cars or motorcycles are left to risk their lives on roads that barely accommodate pedestrians. Those who can drive claim an ever-larger share of public space, while walking becomes a leisure activity confined to gated communities, parks or gym treadmills. In a country grappling with rising obesity and lifestyle diseases, cities have turned the most basic form of exercise into something not just inconvenient, but too often dangerous. Clearly, making people walk will require far more than a court order. "Walking as a fundamental right should lead to pedestrian-friendly cities, not just pedestrian-friendly streets," says Tiwari. That means rethinking how cities are designed. Some countries have adopted default urban speed limits of 30km/h or 20mph to protect pedestrians, regardless of the type of road. Achieving that, Tiwari says, requires redesigning streets by narrowing traffic lanes, altering road surfaces and introducing other traffic-calming measures. The judges also reflected on walking as something far greater than a way of getting from one place to another. It can be "necessity for the poor, meditation for some, an act of resistance for others and a path to discovery. Walking, they noted, also helped shape India's freedom struggle". As writer Sumana Roy notes, external, India's political history has often unfolded on foot -from Gandhi's "salt march" to Dandi to Subhas Chandra Bose's "Delhi Chalo" (March to Delhi) and the many protest marches that followed. For Tiwari, that broader understanding of walking should also shape how cities are built. "Walking is more than a travel option," she says. "Therefore a safe walking infrastructure requires more than creating footpaths and safe crossing. Walking spaces have to integrate activities like spaces of street vendors, shaded paths, areas for resting for old people and sometimes space where children can play." For decades, Indian cities have asked how to move more vehicles. The top court has reminded them to ask a simpler one: how do people walk? I'd settle for something wonderfully unremarkable: a footpath that simply carries me from one end of the street to the other. - Published17 November 2024

item.title: Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78g3glpl8wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? - Published For now, beleaguered Fifa president Gianni Infantino still has some allies in world football, particularly in parts of the world where less well-off football associations have benefited from his presidency. Infantino's position has been under scrutiny since his controversial plan to sell stakes in Fifa's global competitions to private investors was scrapped having been opposed by some regional governing bodies. Late on Thursday, the executive committee of the African confederation (Caf) unanimously confirmed its support for Infantino, after leading African football administrators sent messages backing him. Five of the seven African countries on the Fifa Council - Egypt, Morocco, Niger, Mauritania and Comoros - have already supported him publicly. Support from the continent largely stems from Fifa's Forward programme, a funding scheme Infantino introduced in 2016 that many African federations have become increasingly reliant on to fund football projects in areas where commercial and government investment in the sport is limited. Our reporters and correspondents have explained below where some of Africa's key footballing nations stand. - Faisal Islam: Four reasons why Fifa's World Cup plan never stacked up - Published5 days ago Morocco Morocco's rise as one of Africa's football success stories has largely been driven by government funding, but the country has also become a key partner for Fifa. Morocco's capital, Rabat, is home to Fifa's Africa regional office, they have hosted Fifa Club World Cups, a women's U17 World Cup and will co-host the men's 2030 World Cup alongside Spain and Portugal. Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) president Fouzi Lekjaa reaffirmed his support for Infantino after he withdrew the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal last week. In a statement, Lekjaa described Infantino's decision to withdraw it as "wise", adding it put the unity of Fifa's 211 member associations first. Infantino also received the backing of senior football executives at a meeting in Morocco on Wednesday, following a turbulent period after the proposal's collapse. Reporting by Celestine Karoney Egypt Egypt is home to the Confederation of African Football headquarters and remains one of Infantino's strongest institutional allies in Africa. The relationship is reinforced by the influence of Hany Abo Rida, a Fifa Council member and one of the continent's most prominent football administrators, who has maintained close ties with Infantino since his election in 2016. During Infantino's presidency, Egypt has benefited from Fifa's Forward programme, which has funded infrastructure projects, youth development, coach education and women's football. Like other African member associations, the Egyptian Football Association has also received increased development funding under Fifa's expanded investment strategy, while new and expanded football competitions have created additional commercial and sporting opportunities. But support for Infantino in Egypt is accompanied by growing expectations. Officials and observers increasingly argue that Fifa's engagement with Africa should extend beyond financial assistance. Greater emphasis is being placed on good governance, transparency, sustainable football development and giving Cafmore room to shape the continent's own priorities. Reporting by Mohamed Alkaaoud in Cairo DR Congo The Congolese Football Federation (Fecofa) has welcomed Infantino's decision to withdraw the controversial Forward Enterprise proposal, calling it "wise" in a statement earlier this month. Pointing to a decade of work promoting football worldwide - and in particular his support of African nations - the federation stressed that the episode should not overshadow Infantino's wider record. Fecofa stressed that the episode, born of good intentions, should not overshadow Infantino's wider record. It pointed to his decade of work promoting football worldwide, and particularly his support for African federations and those with fewer resources. The federation said it had "greatly benefited" from Fifa's programmes, citing investment in development and infrastructure. The declaration was signed by Véron Mosengo‑Omba, elected president of Fecofa in May 2026. His election ended a period of uncertainty following the resignation of Constant Omari Selemani in 2021 and the subsequent Fifa‑appointed Normalisation Committee established in April 2023. Mosengo‑Omba assured Infantino of Fecofa's "full support" would continue beyond 2027, recalling mandates renewed in Paris in 2019 and Kigali in 2023. The statement underlines the Democratic Republic of Congo's alignment with Fifa leadership at a time when divisions remain sharp elsewhere in world football. Reporting by Emery Makumeno Nigeria The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has largely aligned itself towards a supportive stance for Infantino's leadership, despite the wider backlash globally. For a football federation facing chronic funding constraints and enormous infrastructure needs, Infantino's proposed plans would have been difficult to dismiss. Former president of the NFF and deputy chairman of Fifa's Men's National Teams Competitions Committee, Amaju Pinnick, argued that Infantino's plan would deliver a much-needed financial boost to every member association without over-relying on local governments. Nigeria is eligible for up to $8m (£5.95m), for the current Fifa Forward funding, despite failing to qualify for the last two men's World Cup tournaments. The most prominent Forward project currently under way in Nigeria is the redevelopment of the NFF Technical Centre in the capital, Abuja. The project, funded with approximately $4.88m, includes the reconstruction of training pitches, and the construction of a modern accommodation complex for Nigeria's national teams. Reporting by Emmanuel Akindubuwa What others in Africa have said The Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture of South Africa, Gayton McKenzie, posted on X saying that Infantino had been "very good to African football". "Africa should be cautious in joining the public lynching of Infantino. He has been very good to African football. "We can debate his ideas but let's not forget who has been a friend to us. Many of those calling for his head want the old status quo back too." Speaking to the BBC after Infantino's proposal emerged, football officials from Malawi and Uganda said Fifa investment had transformed the game both on and off the pitch, arguing such funding is vital given the financial realities facing many African nations. "Malawi needs money. Malawi needs stadiums, our government cannot manage to give us even $1m every year for football," Malawi FA president Fleetwood Haiya told BBC's Newsday programme. "Our government is not able to make sure that they have medical supplies in hospitals [and] at the same time to look at football," he said. President of the Gambia Football Federation, Lamin Kaba Bajo, told BBC Sport: "As far as I'm concerned, most of my colleagues are concerned, we'll encourage him [Infantino] to stay, and we'll do everything within our means to ensure that he is re-elected come next year, 2027. "That's my personal opinion as president of the federation, and a good number of African memberships also stand on that line. He is here to stay." But support for the project on the continent was not universal. Former Sierra Leone FA president and ex-Fifa Council member Isha Johansen was among African voices opposing it, warning it risked over-commercialising football asking, "What price does one have to pay in order to get to this elevated development for football in Africa?" Johansen urged African football chiefs to think carefully about the game's future. Last month, Caf president Patrice Motsepe lauded Infantino for his "excellent work" after this year's World Cup and hailed him as "a good friend". "He is loyal to Africa," Motsepe said on 22 July. "When people have been loyal to you, you never stab them in the back." Other nations are yet to comment publicly, including Senegal, whose men's team is the second-highest ranked African team behind Morocco.

item.title: Livestreamer's murder raises questions over relations between Mexico's creators and cartels
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg9dwz8p30o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Livestreamer's murder raises questions over relations between Mexico's creators and cartels - Published The killing of a young influencer, caught on camera as he was livestreaming in Mexico's Sinaloa state, has raised questions about possible links between content creators and criminal cartels in this violence-wracked part of the country. On the stream, two men on a motorbike can be seen riding up to César Gastélum, who is chatting to two friends outside a fast food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. The murder happens within seconds: the driver of the bike shoots him in the head at close range before fleeing. While the Sinaloa state prosecutor's office provided little detail about the incident, it did say that its lines of investigations included a number of posts Gastélum had published, "some of which refer to a criminal group". Gastélum is not the first influencer to be murdered in Sinaloa. At least 10 content creators have been killed in the state since a deadly war broke out between two rival factions of the Sinaloa criminal cartel two years ago. Officials say Gastélum had not received any threats from criminal groups, nor was he under investigation by police for any alleged criminal links, as had been the case with some of the influencers targeted in the past. But according to Claudia Arruñada, a communications expert at Mexico's Iberoamerican University, the worlds of social media and the criminal underworld can sometimes become intertwined - with at times deadly consequences. "The [social media] algorithm and the narcos promote the same thing: consumption and luxury as ultimate values, to be achieved in the quickest way possible." "The model for success is no longer based on methodically working on your career, but rather on having a meteoric rise," she adds. Arruñada argues that in some cases influencers have promoted narcoculture, by showing luxurious lifestyles to their followers and linking these riches to the exploits of narcos. Gastélum often shared pictures of himself posing with expensive cars, enjoying the nightlife and going on luxury trips, as well as comedy clips and challenges. In one photo he posted, he could be seen at the grave of Leobardo Aispuro, better known as "El Gordo Peruci", an influencer who was murdered in 2024. Content creators like him have vehemently rejected being labelled as "narco-influencers", arguing that the sheer fact of being a young public figure showing off a luxury lifestyle can make you a target in Culiacán. Some studies suggest that the cartels - which function very much like multinational companies with various business interests - do use content creators as community managers, to promote their "brand". When rival factions turn on each other, those seen as spreading propaganda for one group can quickly become targets for its sworn enemies. This is what appears to have happened in January 2025, when leaflets were dropped from an aircraft onto the streets of Culiacán. The pamphlets accused 25 influencers and musicians of having links to "La Mayiza", a faction of the Sinaloa cartel involved in a deadly confrontation with rivals "Los Chapitos". Four of those named had already been killed and were marked on the leaflet as "eliminated". Two more have been murdered since. Gastélum's name was not on that list but his killing is nevertheless seen as the latest in a trend seeing influencers being targeted. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Wednesday that local and national authorities would go after those who had murdered him - and those who had ordered it. Her government is trying to sever the link between popular culture and the criminal underworld, denouncing narcocorridos, songs which glorify criminals, as well as tackling crime head on. Official figures suggest the number of murders fell by 48% in 2025. But there is little doubt that killings like that of Gastélum - witnessed by his followers who were online at the time as it unfolded - strengthen the impression that narcos continue to wield power - and death - not just on the streets of Culiacán but also on digital platforms.
